opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most interesting open questions right now, because what worked for language doesn't transfer to vision as directly as people hoped.

In math or code, long chain-of-thought works because the reasoning lives naturally in text. You write down a step, check it, backtrack, try another path. Text is both the medium of thought and the medium of verification. When people first applied the same recipe to multimodal models, they mostly did this: look at the image once, turn it into an internal representation, then reason in language for a long time. That helps on some benchmarks, especially ones that are really math problems with a diagram attached. But for genuine visual understanding I don't think it's the right shape.

The problem is that the image gets "read" only once, at the beginning. Everything after that is reasoning over a lossy summary. Humans don't work that way. When you look at a complicated scene, a chart, or a maze, your eyes keep moving. You form a hypothesis, then go back and look at a specific region to check it. Perception and reasoning are interleaved. So I think long chains of thought for vision should include actions on the image itself: zooming in, cropping, re-attending to a region, maybe drawing an auxiliary line or marking something, then looking again. The chain of thought should be a sequence of thinking and looking, not just a long monologue after a single glance.

The second point is about what the intermediate states are. In language, intermediate steps are tokens, and that's convenient. For vision, some intermediate steps are inherently spatial or visual. If you're mentally rotating an object or tracing a path, forcing that into words is awkward and loses information. So there's a real question of whether the model should be able to "think in images," generating or editing visual intermediate representations as part of its reasoning. I think that's where things need to go eventually, though it's harder to train and harder to verify.

That connects to the third issue, which is reward. Long chain-of-thought in language took off with reinforcement learning because answers in math and code can be checked automatically. A lot of visual tasks don't have such clean verifiable rewards. Captioning and open-ended description are fuzzy. So part of the work is designing visual tasks where correctness can be checked: counting, localization, spatial relations, puzzles, grounded question answering. That gives RL something solid to optimize, and then you hope the reasoning behavior generalizes.

Finally, I'd say we shouldn't assume longer is always better. In vision a lot of what matters is perception quality. If the base perception is wrong, long reasoning just elaborates on a mistake, and you can even see models talk themselves out of a correct visual impression. So I think the right picture is that the representation and the encoder still matter a great deal, and long reasoning is valuable mainly when it lets the model go back to the pixels and re-examine them. Reasoning that never revisits the image is, in a sense, just language reasoning wearing a visual costume.

r002.rationale: It proposes image actions within the reasoning chain, including zooming, cropping, re-attending to regions, and drawing or marking visual aids.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that we don't yet know, and I'd be suspicious of anyone who claims they do. In language, long chain of thought works because the thinking happens in the same space as the problem. The model reads text, reasons in text, outputs text. Every intermediate step is something it can check and revise in its own medium. Vision doesn't have that property yet. When a model looks at an image and then "thinks" about it, the thinking is almost always happening in language, and language is a very lossy compression of what's actually in the picture. You describe a scene in a few hundred tokens and you've already thrown away most of the information.

So there are roughly two camps. One says: that's fine, just make the language reasoning longer and more careful, and let the model repeatedly go back to the image, zoom in, crop, re-encode the region it cares about. This is a bit like a person squinting and looking again. It works surprisingly well on things like reading small text or counting objects, and I think it's the practical path for the next year or two. But it's a workaround. You're compensating for weak perception by spending inference compute on re-perceiving.

The other camp, which I'm more sympathetic to in the long run, says real visual reasoning should happen in a visual or at least a latent space. If I ask you whether two gears will turn, or how a folded paper will look when unfolded, you don't narrate it to yourself word by word. You simulate it. You manipulate an internal representation. For a model, that would mean intermediate steps that are not tokens of language but something closer to modified images or latent states, and the model learns to roll those forward. Generation and understanding become the same loop. That's why I think the convergence of visual generation and visual understanding is not just an engineering convenience. It might be the mechanism that makes long visual reasoning possible at all.

The hard part is supervision. For text chain of thought, we had an enormous amount of human reasoning written down, and then we had verifiable answers to do RL against. For visual thinking, nobody writes down their visual reasoning, because there's nothing to write. So you have to construct tasks where the final answer is checkable, and let the model discover whatever intermediate representation helps. My guess is that's where the breakthrough will come from, not from clever architecture, but from finding enough verifiable visual problems that the model is forced to develop something like imagination.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is that a long chain of thought should stay grounded in the image. You look, form a hypothesis, and then look again to check it. If you only look once and spend a long time reasoning in language, you can build a very elaborate argument around something you misperceived at the beginning.

So I would imagine an iterative process. First understand the overall scene, then identify what matters for the question, inspect those details, and revise your interpretation. For example, if you're trying to understand what someone is doing, you may need to connect their posture, the object in their hand, and the surrounding context. Each step should resolve a specific uncertainty.

And longer isn't necessarily better. For recognizing a simple object, you probably don't need much reasoning. For understanding a complex interaction, you may need several rounds of observation and inference. The important thing is whether the extra computation helps you see and understand something you would otherwise miss.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that a long chain of thought should stay connected to the image. You look, form a hypothesis, and then look again to check it. If you only look once and keep reasoning in language, you can build a very convincing argument on top of a mistaken visual observation.

So I would think of it as a loop between perception and reasoning. For a difficult question, the model might need to focus on a particular region, compare objects, or check a spatial relationship. Each step should help resolve some uncertainty. And if the answer is already clear, there’s no reason to make the chain longer. What matters is whether the additional computation improves visual understanding.
